name: Carlos Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Carlos. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm farm foreman for a contract farming company. The landowner, an old family, pays us to run the place, and I'm the man on the ground. It's four hundred hectares of wheat and oilseed rape plus a hundred and twenty suckler cows, which are beef cows that rear their own calves. I start at half six with the weather and the spray plan, then I'm on the sprayer or the combine in season, and in winter it's the cattle sheds and the hedges.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like a good harvest week when everything runs and the grain's dry. What wears me out is that I'm paid like a tractor driver while I'm running the whole place. I'm also on call as a part-time firefighter in the village, which brings in a bit extra, but with Marta on a school receptionist's wage, two kids and the mortgage, we're never more than a month from trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: a few handy tools and a lot of noise. I use one of those AI apps now and then to check the spray window against the forecast, and it's decent. But I'd say nothing's changed on the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, it means I keep doing what I'm doing for what I'm paid. That's not great, but it's not frightening. My job's safe as long as the company keeps the contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going. I'd ask the company at my review for a proper foreman's rate, which I do every year. And I'd keep the fire service hours because that money is what gets us through January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, because I'd hoped for a bit more help with the paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the paperwork you'd most like rid of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The spray records and the cattle movement forms. I do them at the kitchen table at ten at night. If a program did that, I'd have my evenings back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the contract ending mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The landowner reviews it every three years. If they changed company, I'd probably have to move or find something in the feed mill. That's the real risk, not AI.

S0.say: It's what I expected: a few handy tools and a lot of noise. I check the spray window with an AI app now and then, but nothing's changed on the ground.
S0.think: I keep doing what I'm doing for what I'm paid. That's not great but not frightening, and my job's safe as long as the company keeps the contract.
S0.do: Keeps running the farm and asks again at his annual review for a proper foreman's rate. Keeps his part-time firefighter hours, which cover the family through January.
S0.feel: Calm, a little flat because he'd hoped for more help with the paperwork.
S0.quote: The spray records and the cattle movement forms. I do them at the kitchen table at ten at night.
S0.fieldNote: Carlos talks in measured, practical terms, always weighing costs. His real risk in this picture is the landowner changing contractors, not technology. The firefighting job is a small but important part of how the family gets by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is change you can manage if you're sensible about it. Some jobs on the farm will shrink, sure, but I'd say most farms will take it slowly. Not much point shouting about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd watch the company closely. They run fifteen farms, and if they can run them with fewer foremen and a man in an office with a screen, they will. My worry isn't the work going, it's the number of us needed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait for the company's first trial, probably self-driving tractors on one of the bigger farms. Once I'd seen it work, I'd ask to be trained on it, so I'm the one they keep. I'd also start putting away a hundred a month from the fire service money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not losing sleep, but it's on my mind when I'm on the combine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gareth, the stockman. He's fifty-eight and he doesn't want to learn anything new. If cameras start watching the cattle, he's the one they'll pension off early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait for proof. What if waiting means someone else gets trained first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a fair point. I'd probably put my name down early, just quietly. I wouldn't be the first to use it, but I'd want to be on the list.

S1.say: This is change you can manage if you're sensible. Some farm jobs will shrink, but most farms will take it slowly, so there's not much point shouting.
S1.think: I'd watch the company closely, because they run fifteen farms and would cut foremen if one man with a screen could cover more. My worry isn't the work going, it's how many of us they need.
S1.do: Waits for the company's first self-driving tractor trial and then asks to be trained, quietly putting his name down early. Saves a hundred a month from his firefighting pay.
S1.feel: Uneasy; not losing sleep, but it's on his mind on the combine.
S1.quote: My worry isn't the work going, it's the number of us needed.
S1.fieldNote: He sees the threat precisely: fewer foremen across many farms rather than farming itself vanishing. When pushed on waiting too long, he adjusted gently and said he'd get on the list quietly. He worries for an older colleague who won't adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's come too fast and the government needs to have something ready for people like us. I'd try to keep my head, mind. Panicking online doesn't help anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the company would cut the foremen within a year. If a robot can drive, spray, check cattle and fill in the forms, they need one manager for five farms, and he'll be younger than me. I'd be out with nothing saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut straight away: the second car goes, the satellite TV goes, Lucas's football tour gets put off. I'd ask the fire service for every shift going. And I'd go for anything locally with a wage, the feed mill or the council roads team, before the rush of people like me hit them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd be awake at three going over the numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would those numbers look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mortgage is eight hundred and fifty a month. Marta's wage covers about half of that and the food. Without my wage, we've got about six weeks before something gives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said you'd keep calm in public. Is that hard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's my job to be calm, in the fire service and on the farm. But yes. The calmer I look, the worse it probably is.

S2.say: It's come too fast and the government needs something ready for people like us. I'd try to keep my head, because panicking online helps nobody.
S2.think: I think the company would cut the foremen within a year, with one younger manager covering five farms. I'd be out with nothing saved.
S2.do: Sells the second car, cancels satellite TV and postpones his son's football tour straight away. Takes every firefighting shift and applies for local jobs at the feed mill or the council roads team before others do.
S2.feel: Alarmed, awake at three in the morning going over numbers.
S2.quote: Without my wage, we've got about six weeks before something gives.
S2.fieldNote: His calm public line and private numbers sit far apart, and he admitted it. He knows his exact runway, six weeks, which shows how close the margin is. His side job as a firefighter becomes his main fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is tight but enough to make a plan, and I'd be saying farm companies should retrain their own people before bringing in robots. I'd say it at the company meetings, politely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd still be worried, but I'd have time to make myself the one they keep. I'd be forty-eight when it lands, with Lucas at college age. That's when we'd need money most.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, once the company had a robot on one of the farms, I'd ask to be trained to supervise it. I'd keep putting the fire money aside and pay off the car loan. By year three, I'd want to be the man who manages robots across several farms, not one foreman on one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel more in control. I'd have a list on the fridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes most, going from two years to five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm looking for any job. With five, I can get trained, save a bit and move up instead of out. It's the difference between being pushed and stepping.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Lucas about college?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to study something practical where you deal with people, like nursing or teaching, or even firefighting full time. I wouldn't push him into farming, which my dad did to me.

S3.say: Five years is tight but enough for a plan, and farm companies should retrain their own people before bringing in robots. I'd say it at company meetings, politely.
S3.think: I'd still be worried, but I'd have time to make myself the one they keep. I'd be 48 with Lucas at college age, when we'd need money most.
S3.do: Asks to be trained to supervise robots once the company trials one in the first year. Keeps saving his firefighting pay, pays off the car loan, and aims by year three to manage robots across several farms.
S3.feel: Anxious but more in control, with a plan on the fridge.
S3.quote: It's the difference between being pushed and stepping.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years shift him from scrambling to moving up. His steady style shows: he'd wait for the company trial, then train. He steers his son away from farming, unlike his own father.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent run-up. We should use it to retrain people properly, not just wait. That's about as political as I'd get.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, this one doesn't scare me much. I'd be fifty-three, the kids would be through school, and I'd have years to learn what's needed. It's still the same end, but I'd see it coming like a weather front.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the company's training when it came, and maybe the farm management certificate at the college in the evenings, which I've been meaning to do for years. I'd keep the fire service as long as my knees let me. And I'd try to get the mortgage down a bit faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. Like before a long drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What will you be doing in 2036, do you think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe running robots for the company across a few farms. Maybe teaching. I genuinely don't know what's left when the robots can do it all. I'd guess people still want a person in charge they can shout at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of this you look forward to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not doing the spray records at ten at night. And not having a wet harvest break my back. If the machines take the hard bits and leave me a wage, I'd be glad.

S4.say: Ten years is a decent run-up, and we should use it to retrain people properly instead of waiting. That's about as political as I'd get.
S4.think: This one doesn't scare me much. I'd be 53 with the kids through school and years to learn what's needed, so I'd see it coming like a weather front.
S4.do: Takes the company's robot training when offered and enrols in an evening farm management certificate at the college. Keeps firefighting while his knees allow and pays the mortgage down faster.
S4.feel: Uneasy but steady, like before a long drive.
S4.quote: I'd guess people still want a person in charge they can shout at.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade he's close to calm and even looks forward to losing the paperwork. He's honest that he doesn't know what humans will do once AGI arrives. His plans are modest and steady: training, a certificate and paying down debt.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Six weeks' money and no other farm jobs round here is not a good place to be. What would help is the company being made to retrain people before replacing them, and some short-term support for families like ours while we find our feet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the fire service. In a lot of villages, the part-time firefighters are farmers. If farming goes, who turns out at three in the morning when a barn's on fire?

headlineQuote: If farming goes, who turns out at three in the morning when a barn's on fire?
portrait: Carlos Weber is a 43-year-old farm foreman for a contract farming company, running wheat, oilseed rape and suckler cows, who tops up a low wage as a part-time village firefighter. He uses AI now and then and adopts new kit once it's proven, and his tone is measured even when his numbers are frightening. He's calm in the hype picture and uneasy about steady change, which he sees as needing fewer foremen across many farms. A two-year AGI arrival leaves him with about six weeks of money, while five or ten years let him retrain and aim to manage robots rather than be replaced by them.
biggestWorry: The two-year AGI picture, because his family would have about six weeks of money and there are no other farm jobs nearby.
whatWouldHelp: Farm companies being required to retrain staff before replacing them, plus short-term support for families while they adjust.
